hints: Focus on what has to happen to go all the way from solid sodium to a gaseous ion in one overall change.
First you need $\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$, which is atomisation, then you need $\text{Na(g)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+\text{(g)}$, which is the first ionisation.
Ask yourself whether the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state adds any new information here.
walkthrough:
**See what the overall change really is**

Think of this as the enthalpy of formation of the ion. You start from the element in its standard state, $\text{Na(s)}$, and make one mole of $\text{Na}^+\text{(g)}$.

$$\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+\text{(g)}$$

**Split it into two familiar steps**

You cannot jump directly from solid to ion in one defined term, so split it. First make gaseous atoms, then remove an electron.

$$\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$$ 
This is the enthalpy change of atomisation of sodium, statement 2.

$$\text{Na(g)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+\text{(g)} + e^-$$
This is the first ionisation energy of sodium, statement 1.

**Add the steps with Hess's law**

By Hess's law, the overall enthalpy change is just the sum of the two steps.

$$\Delta H_f[\text{Na}^+\text{(g)}] = \Delta H_{at}[\text{Na}] + IE_1[\text{Na}]$$
So statements 1 and 2 are both required.

**Check statement 3**

Statement 3 is the enthalpy change of formation of sodium itself. By definition, the formation enthalpy of an element in its standard state, $\text{Na(s)}$, is zero.

It is not a step in the route and is not needed for the calculation. Only 1 and 2 are required.

options.A: Incorrect. This option includes 1, 2 and 3. While 1 and 2 are needed, 3 is not needed because the standard enthalpy of formation of $\text{Na(s)}$ is defined as zero and plays no part in the Hess cycle.
options.B: Correct. You need atomisation to get $\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$ and first ionisation energy to get $\text{Na(g)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+\text{(g)}$. Their sum gives the enthalpy of formation of $\text{Na}^+\text{(g)}$.
options.C: Incorrect. This misses statement 1. Without the first ionisation energy you have only made gaseous atoms, $\text{Na(g)}$, not gaseous ions, $\text{Na}^+\text{(g)}$. Statement 3 also adds nothing useful.
options.D: Incorrect. This uses only statement 1. First ionisation energy starts from $\text{Na(g)}$, but you start from $\text{Na(s)}$. You must first atomise the solid, so statement 2 is also essential.
